slides.heading: Welcome: Staying Safe on Every Session
bullets: Know your locations before an emergency happens
Fire, evacuation, elopement, water and heat safety
Floods, earthquakes and medical emergencies
Driving, personal safety and incident reporting
slides.narration: Welcome to Emergency Preparedness and Workplace Safety at Spectrum Squad. At Spectrum Squad, you might work in a family's home, at a school, out in the community, or in our clinic. Each place has its own risks, and here in Las Vegas we deal with extreme heat, flash floods, dust storms, and even the occasional earthquake. In this course you'll learn how to get ready before anything goes wrong, how to handle fires and evacuations, what to do if a child wanders off, how to stay safe around water and heat, how to respond to medical emergencies, and how to protect yourself. We'll finish with how to report incidents. Let's get started.

slides.heading: Know Your Location Before You Start
bullets: Find the exits, fire extinguisher and first-aid kit
Keep emergency contacts and your supervisor's number handy
Know the client's emergency info, allergies and plans
Check this at every new home, school or outing spot
slides.narration: The best time to plan for an emergency is before it happens. Every time you start working in a new location, take a minute to look around. Where are the exits? Where is the fire extinguisher? Where is the first-aid kit? At a family's home, it's okay to ask the parent to show you. Make sure you can quickly reach the parent's phone number, your supervisor's number, and the client's emergency information. That includes allergies, medical conditions, and any seizure or allergy action plan. Picture this. You're starting with a new client in a home you've never visited. Before you open your materials, you ask the parent where the nearest exit is and where they keep the first-aid kit. That small step could save precious time later.

slides.heading: Fire Safety: RACE and PASS
bullets: RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Evacuate
Get yourself and your client out first
PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep
Only fight a small fire if you have a clear way out
slides.narration: If you see fire or smoke, remember the word RACE. R is for rescue, which means getting your client and anyone in immediate danger away from the fire. A is for alarm, so pull the fire alarm if there is one and call nine one one. C is for contain, which means closing doors behind you to slow the fire down. E is for evacuate. Getting out is always the most important thing. Never go back inside for belongings or session materials. If a fire is very small, like a trash can fire, and you have a clear way out behind you, you may use an extinguisher. Remember PASS. Pull the pin. Aim at the base of the fire. Squeeze the handle. Sweep from side to side. If the fire grows or you feel unsure, leave right away.

slides.heading: Evacuating With Your Client
bullets: Stay with your client and keep them in sight
Expect resistance, dropping or bolting
Use calm, simple directions and familiar cues
Go to the meeting spot and tell responders you're out
slides.narration: Evacuating with a child who has autism can be hard. Alarms are loud, and your client may cover their ears, drop to the floor, or try to run. Your job is to stay with your client and keep them in sight the whole time. Use short, calm directions, like walk with me, or outside now. A favorite toy or a first then statement can help them move. If you're in a school or clinic, follow the building's evacuation plan and go to the meeting spot. Once you are out, let staff or firefighters know you and your client are safe. Never leave your client alone to go grab something. If your client won't move and you're in danger, call for help and follow your training and Spectrum Squad's policy.

slides.heading: Elopement: When a Child Wanders Off
bullets: Wandering is a top safety risk for kids with autism
Act immediately: search and call for help
Check water and streets first
Call nine one one fast, then the parent and supervisor
slides.narration: Elopement means a client leaves a safe area without permission. It is one of the biggest safety risks for children with autism, because many are drawn to water or don't understand traffic. Prevention matters most. Keep your client in sight, know where the doors and gates are, and stay between your client and an exit when you can. If a child goes missing, act right away. Don't wait to see if they come back. Search the nearby area and call out for help from anyone close by. Check water first, like pools, ponds, and fountains, and check nearby streets. If the child is not found quickly, or if there is any water or traffic nearby, call nine one one immediately. Then notify the parent and your supervisor.

slides.heading: Water and Drowning Risk
bullets: Drowning is fast and often silent
Know where pools, spas and canals are
Make sure pool gates and doors stay closed
If a child is in water, get help and call nine one one
slides.narration: Many Las Vegas homes and apartment complexes have pools and spas. Drowning can happen in seconds, and it is usually quiet. There may be no splashing or yelling. So when you work at a home with a pool, notice where it is, and check that gates, door locks, and alarms are in place. Never let your client near water without close, active supervision, and only when the activity is part of the plan. Let's say your client loves the backyard, and you notice the pool gate is propped open. Close it, and tell the parent. If you ever find a child in the water, shout for help, call nine one one, and only go in or give rescue breathing if you are trained and it's safe to do so.

slides.heading: Extreme Heat and Heat Illness
bullets: Never leave anyone in a car, not even for a minute
Plan outings early, with shade and water
Check playground surfaces before kids touch them
Heat stroke signs mean call nine one one and cool down
slides.narration: Las Vegas summers are dangerous. The inside of a car can heat up about twenty degrees in just ten minutes, so never leave a child or anyone else in a car, even for a minute. On community outings, go early in the day, bring plenty of water, take shade breaks, and watch the clock. Slides, swings, and pavement can get hot enough to burn skin, so feel surfaces with the back of your hand before your client touches them. Many of our clients can't tell us when they feel sick, so watch closely. Heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, nausea, or cramps can mean heat exhaustion. Move to a cool place and give water. Confusion, hot red skin, or passing out can mean heat stroke. That's an emergency. Call nine one one and cool the person down while you wait.

slides.heading: Flash Floods, Earthquakes and Dust Storms
bullets: Flash flood: turn around, don't drown
Earthquake: drop, cover and hold on
Dust storm driving: pull aside, stay alive
Power outage: stay calm, keep cool, call supervisor
slides.narration: Our desert weather can change fast. During monsoon season, flash floods can fill streets and washes in minutes. Just six inches of moving water can knock a person down, and about a foot can sweep away a car. Remember, turn around, don't drown. Never walk or drive through flooded roads. If the ground starts shaking in an earthquake, drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck under a sturdy table if you can, and hold on until the shaking stops. Help your client do the same, keeping them close. If you're outside, move away from buildings and poles. In a dust storm while driving, pull off the road, turn off your lights, and keep your foot off the brake. If the power goes out, stay calm, keep your client cool, and call your supervisor.

slides.heading: Medical Emergencies
bullets: Serious emergency: call nine one one first
Give only care you are trained to give
Seizure: time it, protect the head, nothing in mouth
Allergic reaction: follow the client's emergency plan
slides.narration: If someone is seriously hurt or sick, call nine one one first. Then give only the care you are trained to give. For a seizure, stay calm and note the time it started. Move hard or sharp things away, cushion the head, and gently roll the person onto their side if you can. Don't hold them down, and never put anything in their mouth. Follow the client's seizure plan, and call nine one one if the seizure lasts longer than five minutes, if it's a first seizure, if the person is hurt, or if they have trouble breathing. For an allergic reaction, follow the client's allergy action plan. Swelling of the lips or face, hives, or trouble breathing can be life threatening. Use an epinephrine auto injector only if you're trained and the plan allows it, and call nine one one.

slides.heading: Driving and Personal Safety
bullets: Never transport clients unless policy authorizes it
Drive focused: seatbelt on, phone down
If a home feels unsafe, leave and call for help
Weapons, violence or threats: get out and call
slides.narration: Many of you drive between sessions. Wear your seatbelt, and put your phone away. Never drive a client anywhere unless it's authorized by Spectrum Squad's policy. A parent asking you for a ride is not enough. Your own safety matters too. If you arrive at a home and something feels wrong, like a fight going on, someone who seems intoxicated and threatening, or a weapon that's out and unsecured, you do not have to stay. Leave, get to a safe place, and call your supervisor. If anyone is in immediate danger, call nine one one. If a client becomes aggressive, give them space, stay out of reach, and keep yourself between the client and the door so you have a way out.

slides.heading: Ergonomics and Safe Behavior Support
bullets: Lift with your legs, keep loads close, don't twist
Ask for help with heavy items
Use only behavior procedures you're trained in
Never improvise physical holds or restraint
slides.narration: A lot of ABA work happens on the floor, at small tables, and with kids who want to be picked up. Protect your body. When you lift, bend your knees, keep the load close, and don't twist. Ask for help with anything heavy, and change positions often during long sessions. Safe behavior support is just as important. Only use the behavior procedures in your client's plan that you've been trained to use. Never make up your own physical hold or restraint, even when things are getting tough. If a client is having severe aggression or self injury and the plan doesn't cover it, keep everyone as safe as you can and contact your supervisor right away.

slides.heading: Incident Reporting
bullets: Report every incident and injury, even small ones
Tell your supervisor the same day
Complete the incident report with clear facts
Notify the parent as your supervisor directs
slides.narration: Every incident and every injury needs to be reported, even if it seems small. That includes a client scratch or bite, a fall, an elopement, an allergic reaction, a car accident, or an injury to you. Tell your supervisor the same day, and complete the incident report. Stick to the facts. Write what happened, when and where it happened, who was involved, and what you did. Leave out guesses or blame. Here's an example. During a session, your client bites your arm and breaks the skin. You might feel like it's no big deal, but you still tell your supervisor before the day ends and fill out the incident report. Reporting protects you, your client, and the family.

slides.heading: Recap and Quiz
bullets: Know exits, first aid and emergency info everywhere
Stay with your client; act fast if they wander
Call nine one one first and give only trained care
Report every incident to your supervisor same day
slides.narration: Great job. Let's review. Know your exits, fire extinguisher, first-aid kit, and your client's emergency information at every location. In a fire, remember RACE and PASS, and always get out first. Stay with your client during an evacuation. If a child wanders off, act right away, check water and streets first, and call nine one one quickly. Watch for heat illness, never leave anyone in a car, and turn around, don't drown. In an earthquake, drop, cover, and hold on. In a medical emergency, call nine one one first and only give care you're trained for. Leave unsafe situations and call for help. And report every incident to your supervisor the same day. Now it's time to take the quiz. You need a score of eighty percent to pass. Good luck.

quiz.question: You're starting with a new client at a home you've never visited. What should you do before beginning the session?
choices: Start right away so you don't lose session time
Find the exits, first-aid kit, fire extinguisher and the client's emergency info
Wait until something goes wrong to ask where things are
Ask the parent to leave so you can focus
quiz.explanation: Planning happens before an emergency. Knowing exits, the first-aid kit, the extinguisher and the client's emergency information saves time when it counts.

quiz.question: During a clinic session, the fire alarm goes off and you smell smoke. Your client drops to the floor and covers their ears. What is your priority?
choices: Go grab your session materials and tablet first
Leave the client and go find the fire
Use the extinguisher on the fire before leaving
Stay with your client and get them out using calm, simple directions
quiz.explanation: Getting out is always the most important thing. Stay with your client, keep them in sight, and use short, calm directions to evacuate.

quiz.question: A small fire starts in a trash can and you have a clear exit behind you. Which describes how to use the extinguisher?
choices: Pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze the handle, sweep side to side
Aim at the top of the flames and spray in one spot
Pull the pin, aim at the smoke, and shake the extinguisher
Squeeze the handle first, then pull the pin
quiz.explanation: PASS stands for Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze and Sweep. Only fight a small fire when you have a clear way out.

quiz.question: At a park, you look up and your client is gone. There is a pond nearby. What should you do?
choices: Wait a few minutes to see if they come back
Call the parent and ask what they want you to do
Search right away, check the pond first, and call nine one one immediately
Finish writing your data, then start looking
quiz.explanation: Elopement near water or traffic is an emergency. Act right away, check water first, call nine one one, then notify the parent and your supervisor.

quiz.question: It's July, and you need to run into a store for two minutes during an outing. Your client is asleep in the car. What do you do?
choices: Leave the car running with the air conditioning on
Never leave the client in the car, not even for a minute
Crack the windows and hurry
Leave the client if a sibling is in the car too
quiz.explanation: A car can heat up about twenty degrees in just ten minutes. Never leave a child or anyone else in a car.

quiz.question: On a summer outing, your client becomes confused, has hot red skin and seems about to pass out. What should you do?
choices: Call nine one one and cool the client down while you wait
Give a snack and keep playing in the shade
Drive the client home to the parent yourself
Wait to see if they feel better in an hour
quiz.explanation: Confusion, hot red skin or passing out can mean heat stroke, which is an emergency. Call nine one one and start cooling the person.

quiz.question: You're driving to a session after a monsoon storm and water is flowing across the road ahead. What should you do?
choices: Drive through slowly since it looks shallow
Drive through fast to avoid stalling
Get out and walk through the water
Turn around and find another route
quiz.explanation: Turn around, don't drown. About a foot of moving water can sweep away a car, and six inches can knock a person down.

quiz.question: Your client has a seizure on the floor during a home session. Which response is correct?
choices: Hold the client down so they stop moving
Put something in their mouth so they don't bite their tongue
Time it, move hard objects away, cushion the head and follow the seizure plan
Leave the room to give them privacy
quiz.explanation: Note the time, protect the head, roll them on their side if you can, and never restrain or put anything in their mouth. Call nine one one if it lasts over five minutes or per the plan.

quiz.question: You arrive at a client's home and two adults are shouting and one is holding a weapon. What should you do?
choices: Leave, get somewhere safe, and call nine one one and your supervisor
Go inside and try to calm everyone down
Wait in the living room and start the session quietly
Take the client with you in your car to keep them safe
quiz.explanation: You do not have to stay in an unsafe situation. Leave, get to a safe place, call nine one one if anyone is in danger, and call your supervisor.

quiz.question: Your client bites your arm and breaks the skin. You feel fine. What should you do?
choices: Nothing, since it was a small injury
Mention it at next month's team meeting
Only tell the parent
Tell your supervisor the same day and complete an incident report
quiz.explanation: Every incident and injury must be reported to your supervisor the same day, with an incident report that sticks to the facts.
